title: The Amazon River
summary: How the Amazon River forms where the Solimões meets the Rio Negro, carries more water than any other river on Earth, floods its forest every year, and shapes life for the villages along its banks.
poll: Living in a village that can only be reached by boat would be more fun than living in a town with roads.

versions.title: A Mighty River
versions.text:
The Amazon is a big river. It is in a hot, wet land. It is very wide. It flows east. It ends at the sea.

It has two main parts. One starts in high hills. One starts in the forest. The two meet. Then they flow as one.

Most land by the river is forest. It is warm. It rains a lot. The river can rise and flood the land.

Each year, heavy rain falls. The river rises. It spreads into the trees. Fish swim in among the trees. Then the water goes down.

No bridge crosses the river. It is too wide. People use boats. They move from place to place in boats.

Many small villages sit by the river. Families fish in it. They travel on it. It gives life to many people.

versions.title: A Mighty River
versions.text:
The Amazon is a big river. It is in South America. It is one of the biggest rivers in the world. It flows east. It ends in the sea.

The river has two main parts. One starts high in the hills, in Peru. The other starts deep in the forest. The two parts meet. Then they flow on as one, bigger river.

Much of the land by the river is thick forest. It is warm and rainy. In the wet season, the river rises and can flood the land.

Each year, heavy rain falls in the wet season. The river rises. It spreads out among the trees. Fish swim in among the flooded trees. After a while, the water goes back down.

No bridge crosses the main river. It is simply too wide. People use boats to cross it and to move from place to place.

Many small villages sit right on its banks. Families who live there fish in the river and travel on it in boats. The big river gives life to many people.

versions.title: The Amazon River
versions.text:
The Amazon River is a huge river in South America. It is one of the biggest rivers on Earth. It is about 6,400 kilometers long. It flows east. At its end, it pours into the sea.

The river forms where two smaller rivers meet. One starts high in the hills. This is in Peru. The other starts deep in the forest. They meet near a village. From there, they flow on as one big river.

Most of the land along the river is thick forest. It rains there almost every day. In the wet season, heavy rain falls. The river rises. It spreads out. It floods the land near it.

Each year, the flooded water spreads in among the trees. Fish swim among the roots. Fish swim among the trunks, too. After some months, the water goes back down. The land dries out again.

No bridge crosses the main river. The river is simply too wide. It is also too far from roads. Instead, people travel by boat. They go from village to village.

Many small villages sit right on the riverbanks. Families who live there fish in the river. They travel on it. They get their drinking water from it.

versions.title: The Amazon River
versions.text:
The Amazon River is a mighty river in South America. It is one of the biggest rivers in the world, about 6,400 kilometers long. Unlike many rivers, it flows mainly east. It ends at the sea.

The main river forms where two large rivers meet. One starts high in the hills of Peru. It carries pale, muddy water. The other starts deep in the forest. It carries dark water. The two rivers meet near a city. From there, they flow on as one.

Much of the land along the river is thick forest. It gets heavy rain almost every day. In the wet season, the river rises. It can flood the land. It can spread far past its banks.

Each year, the rising water spreads in among the trees. This makes a flooded forest. Fish swim among the roots to feed. After some months, the water slowly goes down. Dry land returns once more.

No bridge crosses the main river anywhere along its path. The river is simply too wide. It is also too far from roads. Instead, boats of all sizes carry people and goods. They link small villages that have no roads.

Families who live along the river depend on it every day. They fish in its waters. They travel on it in boats. They get their drinking water from it, too.

versions.title: The Amazon River
versions.text:
The Amazon is a mighty river system in South America. It flows mostly through Brazil. It is about 6,400 kilometers long. It travels east across the land. It ends at the sea.

The main river forms where two large rivers meet. One river begins high in the hills of Peru. It carries pale water full of sediment. The other river begins deep in the forest. It carries dark water. The two rivers converge near a city called Manaus. From there, they flow on as one wider river.

The Amazon is not the longest river on Earth. But it discharges more water than any other river. In fact, it carries more water than the next seven biggest rivers put together. One reason is its huge basin. A basin is the land that drains all its rain into the river. The Amazon's basin covers a vast part of South America.

In the wet season, heavy rain swells the river so much that it rises past its banks. It spreads across the floodplain forest. Fish swim in among the flooded trunks and roots. They feed on fruit that falls from the trees.

No bridge crosses the main river anywhere along its path, because the river is too wide, too far away, and too likely to shift. Instead, boats of all sizes carry people and goods. They link villages that have no roads.

Families along the river depend on it for fishing, travel, trade, and drinking water.

versions.title: The Amazon River
versions.text:
The Amazon is among the most extraordinary rivers on Earth. It stretches about 6,400 kilometers across South America, mostly through Brazil. It is one of the longest rivers in the world, and it carries far more water than any other river, discharging more than the next seven largest rivers combined.

The main Amazon forms where the Solimões and the Rio Negro converge, near the city of Manaus. The Solimões starts high in the Andes Mountains of Peru, carrying pale water, heavy with sediment. The Rio Negro starts deep in the lowland rainforest, carrying much darker water. For several kilometers, the two rivers flow side by side, unmixed, because of differences in temperature, speed, and density. Eventually they blend into a single, far wider channel.

The Amazon's vast watershed is the entire area of land that drains rain and runoff into the river. It covers more than twice the area of India, making it the largest river basin on the planet. More than a thousand smaller tributaries join the main river on its course to the Atlantic Ocean. Each one adds a little more to its already enormous volume, which keeps growing all the way to the coast. Altogether, this single river is responsible for roughly one-fifth of all the river water that empties into the world's oceans, an astonishing share for just one waterway.

During the rainy season, the river rises well beyond its banks and spreads across the surrounding floodplain forest, sometimes turning dry ground into water that is navigable by small boats for many kilometers at a stretch.

No permanent bridge crosses the main Amazon anywhere along its course, largely because the river is so wide, so remote, and so prone to shifting its banks as sediment shifts from one side to the other. Instead, boats of every size connect villages and towns that have no roads reaching them at all, carrying passengers and goods up and down the river each day.

Even far out in the Atlantic, the river's muddy plume and its sheer volume of fresh water measurably change the ocean's salinity for many kilometers beyond its mouth.

versions.title: The Amazon River
versions.text:
The Amazon River system stretches approximately 6,400 kilometers across South America, mostly through Brazil, flowing generally eastward before finally discharging into the Atlantic Ocean through a sediment-rich mouth so vast that its muddy plume is visible from space.

Although the Amazon is not quite the longest river on Earth, it carries, by an overwhelming margin, more water than any other river in existence, a volume so large that researchers describe it as discharging more water than the next seven largest rivers in the world combined. The main river is formed where two of its great tributaries, the pale, sediment-laden Solimões and the nearly black Rio Negro, converge near the city of Manaus and travel side by side for several kilometers, visibly unmixed because of differences in temperature, speed, and density, before finally blending into one continuous, far wider channel.

The Amazon's watershed, the entire expanse of land that funnels rainfall and runoff into the river, covers more than twice the area of India, making it unquestionably the largest river basin on the planet and a defining feature of the entire continent. More than a thousand additional tributaries join the main river along its long journey toward the sea, each contributing to its already enormous volume of water.

During the rainy season, the river rises well beyond its ordinary banks and spreads across the surrounding floodplain forest, sometimes extending many kilometers into low-lying areas and leaving behind water that is easily navigable by small boats among the submerged trees. Partly because of this ever-shifting width and partly because of its remoteness, no permanent bridge crosses the main Amazon anywhere along its course; instead, boats of every size serve as the primary means of transportation, connecting villages and even cities that otherwise have no roads reaching them at all.

Communities along the riverbanks depend heavily on the Amazon for fishing, transportation, trade, and drinking water, and many families have organized their entire way of life around its predictable rising and falling seasons.

Even the smallest tributary feeding into the Amazon ultimately contributes to this staggering volume of water, a volume so immense that it measurably changes the salinity of the Atlantic Ocean for many kilometers beyond the river's mouth. Altogether, this single river system is responsible for roughly one-fifth of all the river water that empties into the world's oceans, an astonishing share of the planet's fresh water moving through just one basin.

All the roads near the river were destroyed by a strong earthquake years ago, and none were rebuilt.

questions.why: The article explains that the river is so wide, so remote, and so prone to shifting banks that no permanent bridge exists, which suggests roads face similar challenges.

wrong.B: The article never mentions a government ban on roads.
wrong.C: The article does not mention an earthquake.
wrong.D: The article does not say people prefer walking.

questions.stem: Why does the article describe fish swimming among the flooded trees?
options: To prove that no fish live in the main river channel during the whole year long
To describe how boats are painted to match the color of the water
To show how the yearly flood becomes part of forest life, not just a danger
To explain why some tributaries are unsafe to drink from in summer
questions.why: By showing fish feeding among the flooded trunks, the article suggests the flood is a normal, useful part of the forest's yearly cycle.

wrong.A: The article does not claim fish avoid the main channel.
wrong.B: The article does not mention boat paint.
wrong.D: The article does not discuss which water is safe to drink.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the river's path from where it forms to the communities along its banks?
options: To list every bridge ever built across the river and the year that each one was finished
To compare the Amazon to the rivers on the other continents of the world
To argue that the Amazon should be renamed after the explorer who found it
To show how the river's features connect to the daily lives of people who depend on it
questions.why: The article traces the river from where it forms through its floods to the communities relying on it, connecting its features to daily life.

wrong.A: The article says no permanent bridge crosses the main river, so there is no such list.
wrong.B: The article does not compare the Amazon to rivers on other continents.
wrong.C: The article never suggests renaming the river.

MID.prompt: Explain two reasons the Amazon carries so much more water than most other rivers, using details from the article.
checklist: I named two reasons the Amazon carries so much water.
I used details from the article to support each reason.
MID.modelAnswer: One reason the Amazon carries so much water is that more than a thousand tributaries join it on its way to the sea, each one adding more water to the main river. Another reason is its enormous drainage basin, which covers more than twice the area of India and collects rain and runoff from a huge part of the continent. Together, these two things explain why the Amazon discharges more water than the next seven largest rivers in the world combined.

keyWords.definition: deep or wide enough for boats to travel on safely
keyWords.example: After the rains, the flooded trail became navigable for small canoes.

keyWords.definition: an area of land where all the water drains toward the same river or lake
keyWords.example: Scientists mapped the watershed to see how pollution might spread downstream.

keyWords.definition: how tightly packed the mass of a substance is, which affects whether it floats, sinks, or stays separate from another substance
keyWords.example: Oil floats on water because its density is lower than water's.

keyWords.definition: the amount of salt dissolved in water
keyWords.example: Scientists measured the salinity of the bay after the heavy rains diluted it.

keyWords.definition: a long, spreading trail of a substance, such as mud or smoke, moving through air or water
keyWords.example: A plume of ash from the volcano drifted for miles across the sky.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Brazil's government has largely failed to connect Amazon villages with modern roads.
The Rio Negro is the only Amazon tributary that carries any sediment at all.
The Amazon's discharge, watershed, and shifting course shape its character and daily life.
The Amazon rainforest contains more plant and animal species than any other ecosystem on Earth.
questions.why: The article traces how the river's volume, watershed, and remoteness shape both its geography and daily life along its banks.

wrong.A: The article explains why roads are difficult to build, but does not blame the government for failing.
wrong.B: The article says the Solimões, not the Rio Negro, carries heavy sediment; the Rio Negro is described as dark instead.
wrong.D: The article is about the river system's hydrology, not rainforest species diversity.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is a watershed?
options: An area of land where water drains toward the same river
A dam built to control a river's seasonal flooding
The exact spot where two tributaries visibly meet
A boat used to carry goods along a navigable river
questions.why: The article describes the watershed as the land that funnels rainfall and runoff into the Amazon.

wrong.B: The article never mentions a dam on the Amazon.
wrong.C: That description matches where the Solimões and Rio Negro converge, not a watershed.
wrong.D: The article defines navigable water, not a boat, elsewhere.

questions.stem: Why do the Solimões and the Rio Negro remain visibly separate for several kilometers after they meet?
options: Because the Rio Negro flows only during the rainy season each year, so it is not always there to mix.
Because a narrow strip of land briefly separates the two rivers underwater, so their waters cannot meet.
Because differences in temperature, speed, and density keep their waters from mixing at once.
Because one of the two rivers is navigable and the other is simply not, so ships keep the waters apart.
questions.why: The article attributes the delayed mixing to differences in temperature, speed, and density between the two rivers.

wrong.A: The article does not say the Rio Negro flows only seasonally.
wrong.B: The article does not mention any underwater land dividing the rivers.
wrong.D: Both rivers are described as navigable waterways.

questions.stem: What does the Amazon's watershed covering more than twice the area of India indicate about the river?
options: That India and the Amazon basin share a border near the sea
That the Amazon basin is the largest river basin on the planet
That the Amazon's basin is shrinking every year, as the rivers dry up
That the Amazon is shorter than most rivers in India, but much wider
questions.why: The article explicitly states that this comparison makes the Amazon's basin unquestionably the largest river basin on the planet.

wrong.A: India and the Amazon basin are on different continents and do not share a border.
wrong.C: The article never says the basin is shrinking.
wrong.D: The article does not compare the Amazon's length to rivers in India.

questions.stem: Which detail from the article best supports the idea that the Amazon affects the ocean far beyond its mouth?
options: Villages along the river depend on it for their daily drinking water.
The Solimões originates high up in the Andes Mountains of Peru.
The river's plume is visible from space and alters ocean salinity for kilometers.
Boats of every size travel the river, from small canoes to large ferries.
questions.why: The article describes the plume reaching far out to sea and notes that the river's volume measurably changes the ocean's salinity beyond its mouth.

wrong.A: This describes a benefit to riverside communities, not an effect on the ocean.
wrong.B: This describes one tributary's source, not an effect on the ocean.
wrong.D: This describes transportation on the river, not its effect on the ocean.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might engineers find it especially difficult to build a permanent bridge across the main Amazon?
options: The riverbed is made entirely of solid rock that no drill can cut, even with strong machines.
No company has ever once expressed any interest in building one, so no plan has been made.
Bridges are against the local law in every single Amazon country, so none can be built.
The river's width, remoteness, and shifting banks would make any fixed design unreliable.
questions.why: The article attributes the lack of a permanent bridge to the river's width, remoteness, and banks that shift as sediment builds up and erodes, which would challenge any fixed structure.

wrong.A: The article discusses shifting sediment, not solid rock.
wrong.B: The article does not discuss company interest or lack of it.
wrong.C: The article never mentions any law banning bridges.

questions.stem: How does the Amazon's seasonal flooding compare with its dry-season state, based on the article?
options: The warm Amazon region freezes completely during part of every year, and the river turns into ice.
It floods only in the dry season and shrinks back in the wet season, when the rains come.
Its width stays exactly the same width throughout the entire year, with no change in any month.
In the wet season it floods the plain; in the dry season it stays within narrower banks.
questions.why: The article describes the river rising and spreading during the rainy season, implying a narrower, more contained state when rains are not swelling it.

wrong.A: The warm, tropical Amazon region does not freeze, according to the article.
wrong.B: The article ties flooding to the rainy season, not the dry season.
wrong.C: The article describes the river's width changing with the seasons.

questions.stem: What is the author's main purpose in the article's final paragraph?
options: To compare the Amazon in an unfavorable way with the Nile River in Egypt.
To describe every single bridge that has ever been proposed for the river, one by one.
To emphasize how small tributaries add up to a volume large enough to affect the ocean.
To argue that scientists ought to stop studying the river altogether, since it is too big.
questions.why: The final paragraph highlights how the combined contribution of tributaries produces a volume so large it alters ocean salinity, underscoring the river's scale.

wrong.A: The article notes the Amazon is not quite the longest river without making an unfavorable comparison to the Nile.
wrong.B: The article states no permanent bridge exists; it does not list proposed bridges.
wrong.D: The article says this phenomenon continues to fascinate scientists, not that study should stop.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the Amazon River's size affects both the land around it and the ocean far beyond its mouth. Use at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained an effect of the Amazon's size on the land around it.
I explained an effect of the Amazon's size on the ocean beyond its mouth.
I used at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The Amazon River's enormous size affects far more than its own channel. On land, its seasonal flooding spreads across the surrounding floodplain forest, sometimes for many kilometers, temporarily turning dry forest floor into shallow water that small boats can cross. Beyond the river itself, its sheer discharge, more water than the next seven largest rivers in the world combined, pushes a sediment-rich plume out into the Atlantic Ocean that is visible from space and measurably changes the ocean's salinity for kilometers from the river's mouth. Both effects show that the Amazon's influence stretches far beyond the villages and tributaries that line its banks.
